subject: Committed GPU pool — true-up ceilings & soft-throttle proposal
messages:
From: Sam Thompson <sam@acmecorp.com>
To: karthik.iyer@redwood.ai
Date: Sun, 2 May 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Committed GPU pool — billing for above-commit usage

Hi Karthik,

Quick question as we're finalizing the SOW and sizing the committed pool: how does Redwood handle usage that goes above the committed throughput? Specifically:

- Is there a hard cutoff (throttle to zero) or a soft throttle where throughput is reduced?
- How are overages metered (per-second, per-minute, per-token)?
- Do you invoice overages in real time or as a monthly true-up?

Our procurement team (cc'd Liza) wants predictable worst-case economics. If possible, can you outline a couple of options (e.g., hard cap + credits vs. soft throttle + monthly true-up) and any pilot-friendly terms?

Thanks — Sam
Sam Thompson
Head of Machine Learning Engineering
AcmeCorp
sam@acmecorp.com

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwood.ai>
To: Sam Thompson <sam@acmecorp.com>
Cc: Liza Wong <liza.procure@acmecorp.com>, laura.bennett@redwood.ai, aditya.rao@redwood.ai
Date: Sun, 2 May 2027 13:05:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Committed GPU pool — billing for above-commit usage

Hi Sam — great questions and thanks for surfacing procurement's constraints. High level, we offer two pragmatic patterns and a recommended pilot option:

1) Soft‑throttle + monthly true‑up (recommended for most customers)
   - During short spikes we allow traffic above commit up to an automatic soft threshold (default 110% sustained over a 10-minute window).
   - Metering: per-minute aggregation with token-level accounting; we round to the nearest minute for billing simplicity.
   - Billing: overages are invoiced at month-end as a true‑up at the agreed overage rate (we can tier the rate by volume).
   - Safety: sustained usage above 150% for longer than 30 minutes triggers an automated capacity alert and temporary tighter throttling to protect other tenants in the dedicated pool.

2) Hard cap + pre-purchased burst credits
   - Traffic above commit is rejected once a hard cap is reached; customer can purchase burst credits in advance which get consumed at a higher rate.

Pilot proposal (what I recommend for Acme):
   - 90-day pilot on a committed pool sized to your 99th percentile baseline.
   - Soft-throttle at 110% with monthly true-up.
   - Overage rate: $2.50 / GPU-hour equivalent (this is a placeholder; final rate subject to commit size).
   - A one-time 10% introductory discount on overage line items for the pilot period.

I've attached a short spreadsheet that maps commit sizes to modeled monthly overage exposure and a playbook for the soft-throttle behaviour.

Attaching: committed_plan_breakdown.xlsx; soft-throttle-playbook.pdf

If that looks reasonable, we can loop in Finance to lock in the exact overage banding and a DocuSign SOW for the pilot.

Best,
Karthik Iyer
Head of Strategic Sales | Redwood Inference
karthik.iyer@redwood.ai

- Pilot overage rate banding (Aditya: can finance support $2.50/GPU-hr equivalent for a 90-day pilot with a 10% intro discount?)

- True-up cadence (monthly is preferred by procurement, confirm no objections)

I've attached the modeling file. If we agree, I plan to propose a DocuSign pilot SOW and include a clause for a 30-day notice to move from soft-throttle to hard cap once the pilot ends.

Thanks — Karthik

[Attachment: committed_plan_breakdown.xlsx]

Karthik — finance can support a pilot at the proposed numbers with the following caveats:

- Pilot overage rate: $2.25 / GPU-hour equivalent (10% reduction from your ask) for 90 days.
- Intro discount: keep the 10% on top of that (effectively $2.03 for pilot).
- Cap on continuous soft-throttle: maximum 2 hours per day per pool; beyond that we move to temporary tighter throttling.
- True-up: monthly invoicing with line-item supporting CSV (we'll attach token counts and minute buckets).

If Acme agrees, Vanessa can own the SOW and DocuSign flow and I'll drop the finance clause into the billing appendix. Recommend we include a 30-day lookback clause to convert historical pilot overages into committed capacity if both parties agree.

—Aditya
